title: Transient Ischaemic Attack: Risk Stratification and Urgent Clinic Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and young people over 16 with a suspected transient ischaemic attack (TIA) seen in primary care or the emergency department: immediate aspirin, referral for specialist assessment within 24 hours, imaging and carotid pathway. Checked against NICE NG128 recommendations 1.1.1–1.1.7 and 1.2.1–1.2.6.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi national TIA or stroke guideline was opened for this version; every threshold and timing is NICE NG128.
Short-course dual antiplatelet therapy and long-term secondary prevention drug choices sit in NICE technology appraisals and the secondary-prevention section, which were not opened here.
Aspirin dose was reused from the repository's earlier stroke topic and cross-checked with NG128 1.1.4; the product label was not re-opened.
Availability of a 24-hour TIA clinic and same-day MRI in Saudi hospitals was not assessed.
SFDA registration and hospital formulary availability were not independently verified.

pathophysiology.summary: A TIA is a temporary focal neurological deficit from brief interruption of blood supply to part of the brain, retina or spinal cord, usually from carotid or cardiac embolism or small-vessel disease (NG128 terms; mechanism summarised from the guideline's carotid and secondary-prevention sections). Symptoms resolve, but the underlying vessel or cardiac source remains, so early recurrent stroke is the risk that drives same-day aspirin and specialist review within 24 hours (NG128 1.1.4–1.1.5). Symptomatic carotid stenosis is the main surgically treatable cause: 50–99% by NASCET criteria or 70–99% by ECST criteria warrants urgent endarterectomy referral (NG128 1.2.4). Scoring systems such as ABCD2 do not reliably identify who will have a stroke, so every suspected TIA is referred urgently regardless of score (NG128 1.1.6).

symptoms: Sudden-onset facial droop, arm weakness or speech disturbance that has resolved or is resolving (NG128 1.1.1).
Sudden neurological symptoms need hypoglycaemia excluded as the cause (NG128 1.1.2).
Other transient focal symptoms such as monocular visual loss, limb numbness or imbalance; record onset time and duration.
physicalSigns: Screen with FAST outside hospital: Face, Arm, Speech, Time (NG128 1.1.1).
In the emergency department use ROSIER to establish the diagnosis rapidly (NG128 1.1.3).
Capillary glucose at the first contact (NG128 1.1.2).
Neurological examination, blood pressure and pulse rhythm to look for cardiac and vascular sources.
redFlags: Persisting neurological deficit or symptoms still present: treat as suspected stroke and admit directly to a specialist acute stroke unit (NG128 1.3.1).
Recurrent episodes or symptoms in crescendo: urgent same-day specialist assessment; do not wait for the 24-hour clinic (NG128 1.1.5).
Suspected alternative diagnosis that a CT scan could detect, such as haemorrhage: arrange CT (NG128 1.2.1).
Capillary glucose low: treat hypoglycaemia first and reassess symptoms (NG128 1.1.2).
precipitants: Carotid atheroma and symptomatic carotid stenosis (NG128 1.2.3–1.2.4).
Hypertension, diabetes, smoking and dyslipidaemia as vascular risk factors addressed under secondary prevention (NG128 1.1.7, 1.2.4).
Cardiac sources such as atrial fibrillation, assessed at specialist review (NG128 1.1.5).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Low capillary glucose with focal symptoms; correct before diagnosing TIA (NG128 1.1.2).
Deficit persists; admit to a specialist acute stroke unit rather than refer to TIA clinic (NG128 1.3.1).
Haemorrhage or mass lesion suspected clinically; CT is justified only when there is such suspicion (NG128 1.2.1).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low glucose explains symptoms; treat and reassess (NG128 1.1.2).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Hypoglycaemia must be excluded as the cause of sudden neurological symptoms before diagnosing TIA (NG128 1.1.2).
ruleIn.normalValue: 4.0–7.8 mmol/L (72–140 mg/dL) random capillary glucose; local ranges apply

ruleIn.testName: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted and blood-sensitive sequences
ruleIn.targetCondition: Territory of ischaemia, haemorrhage or alternative pathology
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Diffusion restriction in a vascular territory supports ischaemia; blood-sensitive sequences show haemorrhage (NG128 1.2.2).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Consider MRI after specialist assessment in the TIA clinic and perform it the same day (NG128 1.2.2).
ruleIn.normalValue: No diffusion restriction, haemorrhage or alternative lesion

references.title: NICE NG128: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Suspected TIA considered a candidate for carotid endarterectomy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Stenosis 50–99% (NASCET) or 70–99% (ECST) with stable symptoms: urgent endarterectomy referral (NG128 1.2.4).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Offer urgent carotid imaging to every candidate; the report must state whether ECST or NASCET criteria were used (NG128 1.2.3, 1.2.6).

references.title: NICE NG128: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Suspected TIA with clinical suspicion of an alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Haemorrhage or mass lesion changes management; not routinely indicated (NG128 1.2.1).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Do not offer CT to people with suspected TIA unless an alternative diagnosis detectable on CT is suspected (NG128 1.2.1).
ruleOut.normalValue: No acute intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion

references.title: NICE NG128: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Adult admitted to the emergency department with suspected stroke or TIA
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A positive score supports a stroke diagnosis and direct stroke-unit admission (NG128 1.1.3).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: NG128 recommends a validated tool such as ROSIER to establish the diagnosis rapidly in the emergency department (NG128 1.1.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and exclude mimics
actions: Screen with FAST outside hospital and ROSIER in the emergency department (NG128 1.1.1, 1.1.3).
Check capillary glucose and treat hypoglycaemia (NG128 1.1.2).
If symptoms persist, treat as stroke and send to a specialist acute stroke unit (NG128 1.3.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Aspirin now
actions: Give aspirin 300 mg daily unless contraindicated (NG128 1.1.4).
Do not wait for imaging or the clinic review to start aspirin (NG128 1.1.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer within 24 hours
actions: Refer immediately for specialist assessment and investigation, to be seen within 24 hours of onset (NG128 1.1.5).
Do not use ABCD2 to set urgency or decide whether to refer (NG128 1.1.6).

clinicalManagement.title: Imaging at the clinic
actions: Do not offer CT unless an alternative diagnosis detectable on CT is suspected (NG128 1.2.1).
Consider same-day MRI after specialist assessment (NG128 1.2.2).
Urgent carotid imaging for endarterectomy candidates (NG128 1.2.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Carotid decision
actions: 50–99% (NASCET) or 70–99% (ECST) with stable symptoms: urgent endarterectomy referral and best medical treatment (NG128 1.2.4).
Below those thresholds: no surgery, best medical treatment (NG128 1.2.5).
Best medical treatment: blood pressure control, antiplatelet, cholesterol lowering by diet and drugs, lifestyle advice (NG128 1.2.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Secondary prevention
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as TIA is confirmed
actions: Offer secondary prevention in addition to aspirin once the diagnosis is confirmed (NG128 1.1.7).
Long-term drug choices follow the specialist plan; see the hypertension and dyslipidaemia topics for titration and statin doses.

regimens.indication: Suspected TIA, started immediately unless contraindicated (NICE NG128 1.1.4)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults and young people over 16 with a suspected TIA
regimens.duration: Start immediately; continue until specialist assessment sets the long-term antiplatelet plan (NG128 1.1.4, 1.1.7)
adjustments: Contraindication to aspirin: NG128 1.1.4 says 'unless contraindicated'; the specialist chooses an alternative
Aspirin-related dyspepsia: consider gastroprotection per local protocol
contraindications: Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulcer

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG128 recommends aspirin 300 mg daily immediately for suspected TIA unless contraindicated (1.1.4). Dose was reused from the repository's earlier stroke topic and agrees with NG128. Short-course dual antiplatelet therapy and long-term antiplatelet choice are specialist decisions not covered here. SFDA registration was not verified. Check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Any suspected TIA is referred immediately for specialist assessment, seen within 24 hours of symptom onset (NG128 1.1.5)
Aspirin 300 mg daily started immediately unless contraindicated (NG128 1.1.4)
Do not use ABCD2 or similar scores to assess risk or set urgency (NG128 1.1.6)
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 50–99% (NASCET) or 70–99% (ECST) with stable symptoms: urgent endarterectomy referral plus best medical treatment (NG128 1.2.4)
Stenosis below 50% (NASCET) or below 70% (ECST): no surgery; best medical treatment (NG128 1.2.5)

teaching.scope: Adults and young people over 16 with a suspected transient ischaemic attack (TIA) seen in primary care or the emergency department: immediate aspirin, referral for specialist assessment within 24 hours, imaging and carotid pathway. Checked against NICE NG128 recommendations 1.1.1–1.1.7 and 1.2.1–1.2.6.
learningObjectives: Start aspirin and refer within 24 hours for every suspected TIA.
Explain why ABCD2 is not used and which patients need carotid imaging.
pitfalls: Delaying referral because the symptoms resolved or a score looked low.
Ordering CT for every suspected TIA.
Carotid reports that do not state ECST or NASCET criteria.
keyPoints: Aspirin 300 mg daily immediately; specialist assessment within 24 hours.
No routine CT; consider same-day MRI after assessment.
Carotid stenosis 50–99% NASCET or 70–99% ECST: urgent endarterectomy referral.

patientEducation: Explain that a TIA is a warning of stroke even though symptoms have gone, so aspirin and review within 24 hours matter (NG128 1.1.4–1.1.5).
Call emergency services at once if symptoms return and use FAST to recognise them (NG128 1.1.1).
lifestyleAndDiet: Stop smoking, reduce salt and alcohol, eat a healthy diet and be active as part of best medical treatment (NG128 1.2.4).
Take blood pressure and cholesterol treatment as advised after the clinic review (NG128 1.2.4).
mdtReferrals: TIA clinic or stroke specialist within 24 hours (NG128 1.1.5).
Vascular surgery for carotid stenosis meeting the endarterectomy thresholds (NG128 1.2.4).
Primary care for blood pressure, lipid and diabetes optimisation.
dischargeCriteria: Aspirin started and the 24-hour specialist appointment confirmed with the patient.
Patient and family can describe FAST and know to call emergency services.
Driving and work advice documented per local rules.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset; secondary prevention started once the diagnosis is confirmed; carotid decision made after urgent imaging (NG128 1.1.5, 1.1.7, 1.2.3–1.2.5).
